The Story of Brahmdatt

I bow with supreme devotion to Lord Jina, worshipped by the world, and I write the story of Brahmdatt so that the righteous may learn from it.

In the city of Kapilya lived a king named Brahmrath. His queen was Ramili — beautiful, learned, and dearer to the king than life itself. Their son was Brahmdatt, the twelfth Chakravarti, who ruled over six continents with ease and justice.

One day, as King Brahmrath sat down to dine, his cook named Vijaysen served him kheer (rice pudding). It was too hot, and the king could not eat it. Enraged at the cook for serving such hot food, the king hurled the very vessel of kheer upon the cook's head. His head was badly scalded, and he died on the spot. Alas! Cursed be such anger, which blinds a man to right and wrong and causes him to commit terrible deeds, for which he suffers endlessly in lower births.

The cook died in great anguish, but the consequences did not end there. He was reborn as a Vyantar deity on the island of Vishalratna in the Salt Ocean. Through his clairvoyant knowledge, he recalled the suffering of his past life and trembled with rage. Disguising himself as an ascetic, he came to the king and presented him with many fruits — bananas, mangoes, apples, oranges, and more. The king, tempted by his tongue, ate them and asked, "Holy one, where did you get these fruits? They are extraordinarily sweet. I have never tasted anything like them. I am greatly pleased with your gift."

The ascetic replied, "Maharaj, my home is on an island. There lies a most beautiful garden, and these are its fruits. Countless more grow there." Hearing these enticing words, the king's mouth watered. He asked to accompany the ascetic to see this wondrous garden. The ascetic agreed, and the king set out with him by ship.

When they reached the middle of the ocean, the deity revealed his true form and seized the king, remembering the cruelty of his past death. He cast the king into the sea. Brahmrath drowned and, due to the heavy sin of killing an innocent man in anger, fell into a lower birth. He suffered for countless ages before eventually being reborn as a human again, where he finally understood the terrible cost of uncontrolled anger and turned to the path of dharma.

The lesson is clear: anger is a fire that consumes the one who harbours it. A king, despite all his power and wealth, was destroyed by a single moment of rage. Those who wish for their own welfare must learn to master their anger, for it leads only to ruin in this life and suffering in the next.
